clue.text: Notify primate about capital abbot originally left

indicators.note: the primate's letters go round the rest, so about signals containment

parts.note: an ape is a primate

indicators.note: left here means departed, so the abbot's initial is taken out of the capital

parts.note: Paris is the French capital

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of the word abbot

explanation.surface: A monkey reports that the abbot has set off from the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' is Paris; 'originally' takes the A of abbot, and 'left' means departed, so that A goes, giving PRIS for 'about' to wrap.
explanation.definitionFit: To apprise someone is to inform them, a formal synonym for notify.

clue.text: Priest at bar ignoring tenth commandment

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving out, so the letter for ten is dropped

parts.note: bar means except, as in 'all bar one'
X is the Roman numeral ten, standing for the tenth

explanation.surface: A priest in a pub breaks the tenth commandment by coveting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' looks like a pub but means except; 'ignoring' drops X from EXCEPT.
explanation.definitionFit: A precept is a rule for action, the sense a moral commandment carries.

clue.text: Station royal detective in big paper

parts.note: R is an abbreviation for royal, as in RN

indicators.note: in places the detective inside the paper size

parts.note: A0 is the largest standard paper size, written AO
DI is a detective inspector

explanation.surface: A royal sleuth features in a broadsheet newspaper station story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'big paper' looks like a broadsheet but is A0, the largest ISO paper size, read as letters AO.
explanation.definitionFit: A radio station is a broadcaster, so a station can mean a radio channel.

clue.text: Monk doesn't start tackling piano like Thomas

indicators.note: tackling means taking on, so the monk's word holds the other letter
not starting means the first letter is removed

parts.note: an ascetic is a person of severe self-denial, like a monk
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A monk who can't begin tackling the piano, just like doubting Thomas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't start' cuts A from ASCETIC; 'tackling' puts P inside. Doubting Thomas would not believe in the Resurrection without seeing proof.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle Thomas doubted until he saw proof, the classic example of a doubter.

clue.text: Let's continue now round the bend to peninsula in Northern Ireland

indicators.note: round the bend means crazy, so the letters of now go mad and rearrange

parts.note: the Ards Peninsula lies in County Down, Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A driver urges pressing on past the bend towards a stretch of coast in Ulster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round the bend' looks like a road direction but means crazy, the anagram signal. The Ards Peninsula is in County Down.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation onwards! is a call to go forward, the same urge as saying we should carry on.

clue.text: No one is against light, entertaining host

indicators.note: entertaining means hosting inside, so the light holds the other letters

parts.note: a neon is a light, as in a neon sign
MC is a master of ceremonies, a host

explanation.surface: Nobody objects to an amusing, sparkling host.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertaining' looks like an adjective for the host but means holding: NEON holds MC.
explanation.definitionFit: Nem con, from Latin nemine contradicente, means with nobody opposing, unanimously.

clue.text: Americans and French kidnap crew for fun

parts.note: Am is an abbreviation for American
US, the United States, stands for Americans

indicators.note: to kidnap is to take and hold, so the French word holds the crew

parts.note: et is the French word for and
a crew is a body of men

explanation.surface: Americans and French abduct a ship's crew just for the fun of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Americans' supplies two abbreviations, Am and US; 'and French' is the French word for and, which 'kidnap' makes hold the crew.
explanation.definitionFit: Amusement is enjoyment or entertainment, a close synonym for fun.

clue.text: Dig the ground hiding lost entrance

indicators.note: hiding means holding concealed inside
ground means crushed or milled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: L stands for lost, as in sports results tables

explanation.surface: Excavate the soil to uncover a buried doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrance' looks like a doorway but is the verb, to enchant. 'ground' rearranges DIGTHE and 'hiding' holds L inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to fill them with wonder, which is to charm and enchant them.

clue.text: Echt, genuine, OK? Possibly not

indicators.note: possibly not as written, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether something is authentic and decides perhaps it isn't.
explanation.walkthrough: Echt is German for genuine; the whole clue also defines the answer, since something said that way is not genuine.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark made ironically is not meant seriously, so its apparent sincerity is not real.

clue.text: Nurse let go right away

indicators.note: away tells us the letter for right is removed

parts.note: to have freed someone is to have let them go

explanation.surface: A nurse was dismissed on the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'away' removes R from FREED.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurse a baby is to feed it at the breast, a verb sense shared by both words.

clue.text: A lot see round new and refurbished rooms opened by university

indicators.note: the see's letters go round everything else, so round signals containment

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city and bishop's see in Cambridgeshire

indicators.note: a word opened by another has that word placed inside it
refurbished rooms are done up anew, so the letters of rooms are rearranged

explanation.surface: Many visitors look over newly renovated rooms at a university building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see' is a bishop's seat; Ely in Cambridgeshire is the usual crossword see. 'refurbished' rearranges rooms, 'opened by' admits U, and 'round' wraps the see about the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Enormously is an adverb of degree meaning very much, just as a lot does in 'it helped a lot'.

clue.text: Boom's touching harbour

parts.note: re means concerning or touching on
a port is a harbour

explanation.surface: Something about a boom near a harbour, like a barrier across the entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a harbour boom, a floating barrier; the definition is the loud noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A report is the loud bang of a gun or explosion, the same thing as a boom.

clue.text: Merchandise comprises, say, German bricks …

indicators.note: comprises means holds within, so the other letters sit inside

parts.note: goods are merchandise
e.g., for example, is signalled by say

explanation.surface: A stock list includes building materials from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bricks' looks like building blocks but is the informal sense of decent, dependable people; the ellipsis links to the next clue, which also deals in bricks.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a brick or a good egg is old British slang praising a reliable, generous person.

clue.text: … one set lengthwise by stone cutter king brought in

indicators.note: brought in tells us the king's letter is put inside

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight
an etcher cuts lines into a plate
R, from Latin rex, stands for king

explanation.surface: Following on from bricks, a mason lays one along its length while a king is brought in.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis continues 13's bricks: the definition is a brick laid lengthwise in a wall. 'cutter' is an etcher, and 'brought in' slips the king between stone and cutter.
explanation.definitionFit: In bricklaying a stretcher is a brick laid with its long side along the face of the wall, unlike a header.

clue.text: Entrenched bridge adversaries scrap over inches

parts.note: in bridge, East and North are opponents at the table

indicators.note: over means covering, so one piece lies around the other

parts.note: a shred is a scrap
in is the abbreviation for inches

explanation.surface: Card-playing rivals squabble endlessly over inches of ground.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, North-South play East-West, so East and North are adversaries. 'over' means covering: the scrap lies over the inches.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enshrined is firmly fixed and preserved, so entrenched in place.

clue.text: Director general's hotline withdrawn

indicators.note: withdrawn means pulled back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: split as hot and line: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps, and a tier is a row or line

explanation.surface: The boss's direct telephone line has been taken out of service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hotline' looks like one word but splits into hot and line; 'withdrawn' turns HTIER around. John Reith was the first Director General of the BBC.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Reith founded the BBC and was its first Director General, so the title names him.

clue.text: Wake in river as marked on map?

parts.note: maps label a river with R. before its name
the Ouse is a river in England

explanation.surface: A boat's wake, apparently charted on a map of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: A map would print 'R. Ouse', giving R and OUSE; the Ouse is a river in Yorkshire and East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: To rouse someone is to wake them from sleep, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Dreamy individuals get wealth he's forfeited

parts.note: one is a single individual
I is the Roman numeral for one, another single individual

indicators.note: forfeited means given up, so these letters are lost

parts.note: riches means wealth
taken as the letters H, E and S

explanation.surface: Starry-eyed people come into money that someone else has had to give up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forfeited' removes HES from RICHES, leaving RIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Oneiric means relating to dreams, from the Greek word oneiros, a dream.

clue.text: English playhouse sure to lose leader Brook

parts.note: NT is the National Theatre in London

indicators.note: losing its leader means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: certain means sure

explanation.surface: A Brook, like director Peter Brook, at an English theatre, about to lose a leading actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brook' looks like the theatre director Peter Brook, but it is a verb meaning tolerate. 'to lose leader' cuts C from CERTAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To brook something is to tolerate or allow it, and to entertain an idea is to admit it for consideration.

clue.text: School cash once collected by no-frills Beeb

indicators.note: collected by means held inside the other piece
no frills means stripped of edges, leaving the middle letters

parts.note: the ducat was a gold coin once used across Europe

explanation.surface: School money from the past is gathered up by the BBC on a budget.
explanation.walkthrough: Beeb is the BBC's nickname; 'no-frills' strips its outer letters. The ducat was an old European coin, 'collected by' the remaining pair.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to teach or train them, which is what educating them means.

clue.text: Pamper popular 16 once, feeding him contents of full English

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: feeding means putting food into, so the letters go inside the other piece

parts.note: DG, director general, was Reith's title at the BBC

indicators.note: the contents of a word are its inner letters

explanation.surface: Spoil a once-popular broadcasting chief by feeding him a full English breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: '16 once' is Reith, once Director General, abbreviated DG; 'him' just refers back to him. A full English is a big cooked British breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: To indulge someone is to gratify their wishes, which is how one would pamper them.

clue.text: Brief about to receive millions?

parts.note: to be in for something is to be about to receive it, as in 'in for a shock'
M stands for million

explanation.surface: A short summary about to land a payout of millions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective but is a verb, to give someone the facts.
explanation.definitionFit: To brief people is to tell them the facts, which is what informing them means.

clue.text: Trim garden centre in outskirts of Redditch

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters between the outer pair
the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters
to garden is to dig over the soil, so the letters of centre are turned over and rearranged

explanation.surface: A plant shop on the edge of a Worcestershire town tidies its displays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'garden' signals ETRENC from CENTRE, placed 'in' RH. Redditch is a town in Worcestershire.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrench is to cut back or reduce spending, and trim can mean exactly that cut.

clue.text: Unity Mitford ultimately wound up in mess

indicators.note: wound up suggests things wound together and tangled, so the letters are rearranged
ultimately points to the last letter of Mitford

explanation.surface: The life of Unity Mitford, one of the famous sisters, ended in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wound up' rearranges UNITY plus D. Unity Mitford was one of the six Mitford sisters, an English aristocratic family.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untidy is in a mess, disordered and unkempt.

clue.text: Coach to cut short corner

indicators.note: cut here means cutting into, so the small word goes inside
short means missing the last letter

parts.note: to corner a car is to turn

explanation.surface: A coach driver takes a corner too tightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims TURN to TUR; TO 'cut' into it gives TU-TO-R. 'Coach' suggests a bus but means a teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutor is a private teacher, and a coach is likewise someone who trains a pupil.

clue.text: £1,000 for each adult to catch opening of Otello or suchlike

indicators.note: to catch means to hold, so the other letter is caught inside

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds
per means for each
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Tickets at a thousand pounds a head for the first night of Verdi's Otello.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to catch' places O, the 'opening of' Otello, between GRAND and PERA. The clue is semi-&lit, Otello doubling as example.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's Otello is a classic example of a fully sung, large-scale serious opera.

clue.text: They've excavated core of smallest artificial mound

indicators.note: excavated means dug out, so only the outer letters of the word are left
the core of a word is its central letters

explanation.surface: Archaeologists have dug out the middle of the smallest barrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excavated' empties THEY'VE to TE; 'core of' takes LL from the middle of SMALLEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A tell is an archaeological mound built up by layers of settlement, especially in the Middle East.

clue.text: Schoolgirl inspiring rebellious Jack

indicators.note: inspiring means breathing in, so the girl takes the rebel inside

parts.note: the girl part of the word gives Amy, a girl's name
Jack Cade led a rebellion against Henry VI in 1450

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl is drawn to a rebellious lad called Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Schoolgirl' must be split: School is the definition and girl gives AMY. Jack Cade led the Kentish revolt of 1450.
explanation.definitionFit: An academy is a school, in Britain especially a state-funded independent secondary school.

clue.text: Trainee lyricist secures a large job

indicators.note: secures means holds fast, so the lyricist's name holds the single letter inside

parts.note: Alan Jay Lerner wrote the lyrics for My Fair Lady

explanation.surface: A trainee songwriter lands a big job.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Jay Lerner, lyricist of My Fair Lady, takes A inside; 'large job' adds L plus EARNER (a money-making job), a second route to the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A learner is someone being taught a skill, which is what a trainee is.
